title: Three events that will decide whether the rally was right
body:
## The vote that clears the table

On June 15, Sivers shareholders will gather to approve a board reshuffled almost entirely for a single purpose: making the company legible to American institutional capital. Three seats are emptying — co-founder Erik Fällström, Vice Chairman Tomas Duffy, and Keith Halsey — and two are being filled by Joakim Nideborn (proposed as Vice Chairman, described in the nomination committee's own circular as a CFO with "broad experience at listed technology companies" and a focus on "capital markets") and Helena Svancar, a corporate-strategy specialist. The remaining board, anchored by Chairman Bami Bastani — a 42-year semiconductor veteran who has run three public-company turnarounds and joined Sivers in August 2023 specifically to architect a US listing — will be a five-person body built for Nasdaq investor days, not Stockholm AGM comfort.

The procedural outcome is not in doubt. The nomination committee's own recommended slate is rarely defeated in Swedish corporate governance. What *is* in doubt is institutional sentiment around the dilution authority that accompanies the reshuffle: shareholders will vote to authorize the issuance of up to 53.8 million new shares, roughly 15% of the existing 311.3 million share float, usable for organic growth, M&A, or — most pointedly — a US listing capital raise. That authority sits alongside a 2% long-term incentive plan, meaning the aggregate authorized dilution pool is meaningful.

The complicating factor is governance, not governance reform. Sweden's Economic Crime Authority (Ekobrottsmyndigheten) is investigating possible market-abuse violations tied to Sivers' Nasdaq listing announcement, which reportedly leaked approximately 48 hours early via an anonymous account on X. The investigation is open as of the snapshot date. Sivers' shares have already more than doubled from their 2025 lows, closing at SEK 72.90 at the frozen window. An AGM that produces the expected board outcome while leaving the Ekobrottsmyndigheten matter unresolved does not close the overhang — it merely defers it.

## The module that must ship

The partnership between Sivers and POET Technologies, announced September 29, 2025, is the structural argument for the entire chokepoint thesis in a single press release. Sivers supplies high-power InP DFB lasers; POET contributes its Optical Interposer platform; together they are building External Light Source modules for co-packaged optics applications in AI data centers.

> "We see a highly complementary fit between our high-performance DFB lasers and POET's innovative optical interposer platform," CEO Vickram Vathulya said at the announcement.

The timeline on paper: early prototypes in H1 2026; production readiness by end-2026. What the timeline on paper cannot capture is module yield rates, thermal performance in sustained operation, and — most critically — named hyperscaler design-in. None of those have been publicly confirmed as of the snapshot date. The ELS market that analyst Tim Savageaux has estimated at over $1 billion annually is real; whether Sivers and POET can capture a material share of it before the next round of capital is required is the execution question that the next six to eight months will answer.

A successful production launch with a named hyperscaler customer in Q4 2026 would validate the entire upstream laser-chokepoint model. A two-quarter slip — plausible given the yield ramp complexities involved in integrating InP lasers with a novel interposer platform — shifts production validation into mid-2027. That timing matters: by mid-2027, Sivers will almost certainly have exercised at least a portion of its new dilution authority, meaning any slip arrives after holders have already been diluted.

## The price that sets the ceiling

The PCAOB restatement completed in May 2026 — which widened FY2025 EBIT loss to SEK 177.8 million from the originally reported SEK 141.3 million, a SEK 36 million worsening driven by revenue reallocation between periods, revised inventory valuations, and impairment of previously capitalized development expenditures — was a prerequisite, not a milestone. The AGM dilution authority is the issuance vehicle. The MSCI Sweden Small Cap inclusion (effective May 29, coinciding with delayed Q1 results) provides a passive-buying tailwind. What remains is the actual listing announcement, still rumored but not yet formal at the snapshot date, and the price at which Sivers raises US dollars.

At SEK 72.90 and 311.3 million shares, the market capitalizes Sivers at roughly SEK 3.4 billion (approximately USD 360 million) against FY2025 PCAOB-restated revenue of SEK 306.6 million — a price-to-sales multiple of approximately 11x trailing. One independent analyst's 2030 bull case, built on 45% annual revenue compounding and a 25% operating margin, arrives at a fair value of SEK 14.52 per share. The gap between SEK 14.52 and SEK 72.90 is not a rounding error; it implies the market is pricing a ramp materially more aggressive than the published bull case supports.

If Sivers prices a US offering at or above the equivalent of SEK 60, it validates the current equity story and locks in a reference point for the next 12 to 18 months. If it prices materially below — because the POET production timeline has slipped, because the Ekobrottsmyndigheten investigation has cooled institutional appetite, or because the PCAOB numbers have complicated the revenue trajectory — the share price has limited support above the offering level.

The bull case requires POET prototypes on schedule in H1 2026, production with a named customer in Q4, FY2026 revenue above SEK 450 million (roughly 50% growth on a PCAOB basis), and an operating loss that narrows below SEK 100 million. The bear case does not require a disaster — only a two-quarter delay on POET, a push-out from the unnamed automotive LiDAR customer (whose platform ramp in Q4 2026 carries SEK 53 to 138 million of lifecycle revenue), and a US listing that prices into a story under construction rather than a story already proven.

Sivers spent 65 years as a passive-microwave shop before two acquisitions in five years turned it into a CPO laser chokepoint. The next 18 months will determine whether the chokepoint is real — or simply early-stage.
